The three ruling houses of the ancient Tamil country in the far south of India: the Cheras on the Malabar coast, the Cholas in the Kaveri river delta, and the Pandyas around Madurai. This bar covers their early age, about 300 BCE to 300 CE, known as the Sangam age.

Ashoka's edicts name the Cholas, Pandyas and Cheras (as Keralaputras) as independent neighbours beyond his empire. Most of what else we know comes from two sources:

  • Sangam literature. Over 2,000 Tamil poems, divided into poems of love (akam) and of war and public life (puram). They describe kings, bards, warriors, farmers and ports. Their dating is uncertain. The Tirukkural, a famous book of short verses on ethics, comes from the same broad tradition.
  • Roman trade. Pepper from the Chera coast, pearls from the Pandya sea, beryl and fine cotton went west. Roman ships sailed to Muziris and other ports on the monsoon winds, and many hoards of Roman coins have been found in south India.

The three houses fought each other constantly and sometimes allied against outsiders. A Chola prince called Elara ruled Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka for decades in the 2nd century BCE. A Chola king, Karikala, is credited with an early dam on the Kaveri.

After about 300 CE the three faded in a dim period ruled by the Kalabhras. The Pallavas rose in the north of the Tamil country, and later the Pandyas and then the Chola Empire came back far stronger.
